# AMC 20-42 — Airworthiness information security risk assessment

> [!summary]
> AMC 20-42 is the acceptable means for assessing the information security risk
> of a product. It asks for a product information security risk assessment, the
> PISRA: identify the assets and the attack paths, judge the safety consequence
> of each threat, and iterate until every residual risk is acceptable. It
> recognises three EUROCAE and RTCA document pairs as acceptable means, and none
> of them is held here. For this engine it carries the whole compliance method
> behind CS-E 50(l).

## Requirement

The verbs are AMC 20-42's own. It is an acceptable means of compliance, so
"should" marks an accepted method and an applicant may propose an alternative
and justify it.

### Purpose and applicability, sections 1 to 3

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **1(a)** | The AMC describes an acceptable means, but not the only means, to show compliance with the applicable rules for the certification of products and parts. | Statement |
| **1(a)** | Compliance with the AMC is not mandatory, and an applicant may elect to use an alternative means of compliance. | Permitted |
| **1(a)** | Any alternative means of compliance must meet the relevant requirements and be accepted by EASA. | Required |
| **1(b)** | The AMC recognises as an acceptable means of compliance EUROCAE ED-202A, Airworthiness Security Process Specification, dated June 2014, with RTCA DO-326A, dated August 2014; EUROCAE ED-203A, Airworthiness Security Methods and Considerations, dated June 2018, with RTCA DO-356, dated June 2018; and EUROCAE ED-204, Information Security Guidance for Continuing Airworthiness, dated June 2014, with RTCA DO-355, dated June 2014. | Accepted method |
| **1(c)** | The AMC establishes guidance to use ED-202A, 203A and 204 in the different contexts of the initial and continued airworthiness of products and parts. | Statement |
| **1(d)** | The possibility to give credit for products developed using previous versions of the EUROCAE ED and RTCA DO documents may be discussed with and accepted by EASA. | Permitted |
| **2** | The AMC applies to manufacturers of products and parts, and to design approval holders that apply for the type certification of a new product, meaning an aircraft, engine or propeller; a supplemental type certificate to an existing type-certified product; a change to a product; the approval of a new item of equipment or a change to equipment to be used in an ETSO article; the certification of other systems or equipment providing air service information whose certification is required by a national regulation; or the approval of products and parts of information systems that are subject to potential information security threats and that could result in unacceptable safety risks. | Statement |
| **2** | Where an ETSO article contains security measures, those measures may be assigned a security assurance level, and the design organisation approval holder can take credit for them and for their associated levels, depending on the information system security risk assessment of the product. | Permitted |
| **3** | Section 3, Replacement, is reserved. | Statement |

### The assessment, sections 4 to 6

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **4(a)** | Assess the information systems of the products, parts or equipment identified in Section 2 against any potential intentional unauthorised electronic interaction (IUEI) security threat and vulnerability that could result in an unsafe condition. That risk assessment is the product information security risk assessment, the PISRA. | Accepted method |
| **4(b)** | The result of the assessment, after any necessary means of mitigation have been identified, should be that either the systems of the product or part have no identifiable vulnerabilities, or those vulnerabilities "cannot be exploited to create a hazard or generate a failure that would have an effect that is deemed to be unacceptable against the certification specification and the acceptable means of compliance including industry standards for the product or part considered". | Accepted method |
| **4(c)** | Where a risk needs to be mitigated, demonstrate that the means of mitigation provide sufficient grounds for evaluating that the residual risk is acceptable, and provide the means of mitigation to the operators in a timely manner. | Accepted method |
| **4(d)** | Once the overall risk has been deemed acceptable, develop instructions as described in Section 9 where necessary, to maintain the information security risk at an acceptable level after the product or part enters into service. | Accepted method |
| **5(a)** | The general PISRA should cover the determination of the security environment for the information security of the product; identification of the assets; identification of the attack paths; assessment of the safety consequences of the threat to the affected assets; evaluation, by considering the existing security protection means, of the level of threat that would have an impact on safety; determination of whether the risks are acceptable, those risks being the combination of the severities and the potentiality to attack, or inversely the difficulty of attacking; and iteration until all the residual risks are acceptable. | Accepted method |
| **5(a)(vi)** | Where the risks are acceptable, prepare the justification for certification, including the means to maintain the risk at an acceptable level. Where they are not, analyse the proposed means of mitigation to ensure an acceptable level of safety, implement them, and evaluate their effectiveness with respect to the level of risk. | Accepted method |
| **5(b)** | The process for the Security Risk Assessment identified in ED-202A Section 2.1.1 is an acceptable means of compliance for performing the PISRA for products and parts under Annex I (Part 21) to Regulation (EU) No 748/2012. Guidance material for the PISRA can be found in ED-203A. | Accepted method |
| **6** | Whether or not a risk is unacceptable depends on the context and the criteria that are considered for the certification of the affected product or part. The same risk may be acceptable in some cases and unacceptable in others. | Statement |

### After the assessment, sections 7 to 10

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **7** | The operator of a product or part should report any information security occurrence to the designer of that product or part, or to the aircraft type certificate or supplemental type certificate holder, in a manner that would allow a further impact analysis and corrective actions. | Accepted method |
| **7** | Where the impact analysis identifies the potential for an unsafe condition, the designer should report it to the competent authority in a timely manner. For organisations to which Regulation (EU) No 748/2012 applies, the reporting should be done in accordance with point 21.A.3A of Annex I (Part 21). | Accepted method |
| **8** | Where information security risks identified during the PISRA need to be mitigated, use security verification to evaluate the effectiveness of the means of mitigation: by a combination of analysis, security-oriented robustness testing, inspections and reviews, and, when necessary, by security testing that addresses information security from the perspective of a potential adversary. | Accepted method |
| **9** | Identify the information security assets and protection mechanisms to be addressed by the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness of the product or part, and develop the appropriate procedures to maintain the security effectiveness after the product or part enters into service. | Accepted method |
| **9** | Where an in-service occurrence is reported, consider the possibility that it originated from an IUEI and take any required corrective action. Where an IUEI has generated an unsafe condition, report the occurrence, the investigation results and the recovery actions to EASA in accordance with point 21.A.3A of Annex I (Part 21). | Accepted method |
| **9** | An occurrence is defined by Article 2(7) of Regulation (EU) No 376/2014 as any safety-related event which endangers, or which, if not corrected or addressed, could endanger an aircraft, its occupants or any other person, and includes in particular any accident or serious incident. Article 4 of the same Regulation requires the applicant to report to EASA any occurrence that represents a significant risk to aviation safety. | Statement |
| **9** | Assess the impact of new threats that were not foreseen during previous PISRAs. Where the assessment identifies an unacceptable threat condition, notify the operators and the competent authority in a timely manner of the need and the means to mitigate the new risk, or of the absence of a risk. | Accepted method |
| **9** | Guidance on continued airworthiness can be found in EUROCAE ED-203A with RTCA DO-356A, and in ED-204 with RTCA DO-355. | Statement |
| **10** | The terminology used in the AMC is consistent with the glossary provided in EUROCAE ER 013, Aeronautical Information System Security Glossary. | Statement |

The last row of section 9 names DO-356A, where section 1(b) recognises DO-356
dated June 2018. Both spellings are the source's own and are copied as written
[ext AMC 20-42 1(b)], [ext AMC 20-42 9].

Section 6 gives the one worked example in the document, and it turns on the code
the product is certified to. A threat condition with a potential major safety
effect, as defined in CS xx.1309, "may be not acceptable in the context of CS-25
products depending on the level of threat and the associated threat scenario",
while "The same safety risk may be acceptable for products that are certified
under CS-29" [ext AMC 20-42 6]. The AMC names CS-25 and CS-29 there. It does not
name CS-27, and the vault does not supply it.

## Bearing on this engine

**The engine is a product this AMC applies to.** Section 2 reaches a design
approval holder applying for "the type certification of a new product (i.e. an
aircraft, engine or propeller)" [ext AMC 20-42 2]. The AMC is therefore read at
engine level and not only at aircraft level, which is what makes it usable as
the means for a CS-E obligation.

**It is the whole method behind one CS-E sub-point.** [[CS-E 50|CS-E 50(l)]]
requires the information system security protection, and the AMC to CS-E 50(l)
hands the method to AMC 20-42 and adds one scoping condition of its own: the
assessment also takes into account IUEIs that could have similar effects on all
the Engine Control Systems of an aircraft. That condition, and the compliance
items that follow from it, are recorded in [[AMC E 50]]. The engine declares a
full-authority EECS in a multi-engine installation, so every engine carries the
same control system and the common-mode case is real.

**The attack paths run through the aircraft interfaces.** Step three of the
PISRA is the identification of the attack paths [ext AMC 20-42 5(a)]. On this
engine the control system depends on aircraft-supplied data and on
aircraft-supplied electrical power, which are the subject of
[[CS-E 50|CS-E 50(g)]] and [[CS-E 50|CS-E 50(h)]] and are interfaces declared
under [[CS-E 20]]. The assumptions behind them belong to [[CS-E 30]].

**Two duties outlive certification.** The assets and protection mechanisms are
identified for the Instructions for Continued Airworthiness, with procedures to
maintain their effectiveness in service [ext AMC 20-42 9]; that is an input to
[[CS-E 25]]. And a reported in-service occurrence is considered for the
possibility that it originated from an IUEI, with reporting under point 21.A.3A
where an unsafe condition has been generated [ext AMC 20-42 9]. That reporting
route is the one recorded in [[AMC E 515]].

[VERIFY: which certification context sets the acceptability criterion for this
engine. Section 6 makes acceptability depend on the code the affected product is
certified to, and contrasts a CS-25 product with a CS-29 one
[ext AMC 20-42 6]. The engine is certified under CS-E, and the installation
under CS-27 or CS-29; `engine_profile.md` does not fix the airframe code, which
is the open item in [[CS-E 30]]. The AMC does not say which context governs an
engine certified separately from its aircraft.]

The method inside the process is a dead end here. ED-202A with DO-326A, ED-203A
with DO-356, ED-204 with DO-355 and the ER 013 glossary are sold by their
publishers, and no paywalled material is committed to this repository. This note
records the process AMC 20-42 states and stops at the point where it defers.
`review/dead_ends.md` lists what that leaves unstated.
